# INNOVA 5610 STUCK on follow instructions on PC

When an Innova 5610 diagnostic tool updates successfully to the latest firmware, bootloader, and database, you expect immediate connectivity. Instead, many users encounter a specific failure mode where the device screen freezes on "Follow instructions on the PC." In this state, the hardware appears powered, but the software logic has halted before establishing a handshake with the vehicle or the host computer. The user interface becomes unresponsive to button presses, and the standard navigation menu fails to render. This behavior suggests the bootloader is waiting for a specific packet from the PC that never arrives, effectively trapping the device in an idle loop.

The root cause often lies in the communication protocol between the diagnostic tool and the host operating system. The Innova 5610 relies on a virtual COM port (VCP) or a USB-to-Serial bridge to transmit data packets containing vehicle identification numbers (VIN) and session commands. If the PC does not present the correct driver signature or if the serial baud rate configuration mismatches the firmware's expectations, the bootloader cannot validate the incoming handshake. Consequently, it defaults to a safe state message: "Follow instructions on the PC," waiting indefinitely for input that will never come from a misconfigured connection.

To resolve this, you must first verify the virtual port availability within your operating system. On Windows, open the Device Manager and navigate to the Ports (COM & LPT) section. You should see an entry corresponding to the Innova device, typically labeled as "USB Serial Port" or similar. If this entry is missing or shows a yellow exclamation mark, the VCP driver installation failed during the update process. Reinstalling the specific driver provided by the manufacturer is mandatory; generic serial drivers often lack the proprietary handshake routines required by the Innova bootloader.

Once the physical connection and driver stack are confirmed, examine the communication settings in your diagnostic software. The baud rate must match exactly between the PC application and the tool's firmware configuration. A common pitfall occurs when updating the database but failing to reset the communication parameters. If the tool expects a 9600 or 115200 baud rate with specific parity settings, and the PC software defaults to different values, the data stream becomes corrupted immediately. The bootloader detects this corruption and halts execution, displaying the static message to prevent further damage.

In some instances, the issue stems from the USB host controller not properly enumerating the device in a low-power state. Disconnecting the power supply completely for at least 30 seconds allows the internal capacitors to discharge, clearing any stuck states in the microcontroller's memory buffer. This hard reset forces the bootloader to re-initialize its pin multiplexing and re-attempt the handshake sequence upon reconnecting.

If these steps fail, consider flashing the bootloader directly via a known-good serial adapter connected to the tool's debug interface, bypassing the faulty USB-COM bridge entirely. This approach isolates whether the issue is with the main USB controller or the internal logic handling the "Follow instructions" prompt. By injecting a raw initialization command sequence directly into the reset vector, you can force the device out of the waiting loop and re-establish communication channels without relying on the high-level PC interface initially.
